endorsements.quote: The European General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and similar frameworks establish principles, including data minimization, purpose limitation, and transparency, which should guide digital biomarker development [ 77 ].
Clinical decision support tools must integrate these digital biomarkers with existing clinical data streams, providing evidence-ranked recommendations personalized to individual patient phenotypes.
Patient engagement throughout development and implementation is essential for creating acceptable and effective monitoring systems.

unlisted_practices: Prioritize accessible user interface design with adjustable features accommodating visual, motor, and cognitive limitations in digital monitoring tools.
Use hybrid approaches combining digital and traditional monitoring to serve diverse patient populations.
Apply privacy-by-design principles, including differential privacy, federated learning, and on-device processing, to digital biomarker systems.
Validate digital biomarkers against established clinical measures, neuroimaging, performance measures, and patient-reported experience using a multimodal approach.
Use explainable AI approaches rather than black-box models to support clinical adoption.
Use personalized baselines and recalibrate composite fatigue metrics regularly to account for disease progression.
Use participatory design involving patients as co-developers of monitoring systems.
Address attrition bias in digital monitoring studies using adaptive monitoring, joint modeling of dropout, and sensitivity analyses.

screen.reason: This is a perspective paper proposing a framework and discussing implementation considerations (privacy, equity, regulatory pathways) for digital biomarkers and AI for remote monitoring of fatigue.
